sm: This Potomac Watch episode from the Wall Street Journal opinion pages, hosted by Paul Gigot with Kate O'Dell and Allysia Finley, begins with the three-way summit among President Trump, Vladimir Putin, and Xi Jinping. O'Dell says the best that can be said is that it could have been much worse, since little concrete was achieved and Ukraine and Iran reportedly did not come up in the trilateral portion. She says Trump wants to show leadership on the world stage and start arms control talks, but China is in one of history's great nuclear buildups and is uninterested. She adds that Putin has rattled nuclear sabers and left earlier treaties, and that Russia and China tacitly help Iran.

The discussion continues with Gigot recalling the arms control fights of the 1970s and 80s and saying the agreements came because the Soviets concluded they could not win a competition with America. O'Dell says the foundation for such a deal does not exist now, since China is building up and the military has not been rebuilt as promised. She notes that Trump's 1.5 trillion dollar Pentagon budget request is in trouble on Capitol Hill. She says Trump could speed up a sea-launched nuclear cruise missile to counter Russian tactical nuclear weapons and avoid nuclear blackmail. The segment then turns to the Anthropic public offering, priced at 83 dollars a share for a 1.5 trillion dollar valuation, with shares popping as high as 33 percent before settling about 16 percent higher.

Finley says demand for Anthropic shares came despite a week of gloom over Nvidia, after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, because investors see Anthropic at the frontier of commercializing AI. She says the offering will create many millionaires, with a report that about 600 of roughly 5,000 employees will hold over 100 million dollars in shares, and will give California a tax windfall. Index funds and pension funds will own shares as Anthropic joins major indexes. She notes public unease about AI and data centers, and says CEO Dario Amodei's warnings about job losses feed it. She lists risks including competition from OpenAI, Google, Meta, and xAI, plus regulation and a cybersecurity event.
